outputs.L1: An electric-drive dump truck travels by receiving electrical power from trolley lines through power collection units that are raised and lowered by lifting devices and brought into contact with the trolley lines. A position detection device detects the position of the electric-drive dump truck, while a vehicle speed detection device detects its speed. A storage section stores the position of the trolley lines and the time required for the power collection units to contact the trolley lines after beginning to rise (hereinafter referred to as the “moving-up time”). Based on the position and speed of the electric-drive dump truck, the position of the trolley lines, and the moving-up time, a control device outputs a signal indicating that the power collection units may be raised.
outputs.L2: An electrically driven dump truck is propelled by electrical power obtained from trolley lines through current-collecting units that lifting mechanisms can raise and lower. A position detector determines the truck’s location, while a speed detector measures its traveling speed. A storage unit retains information identifying the location of the trolley lines and the period required for the current-collecting units to reach and contact the trolley lines after beginning to rise, referred to as the “raising time.” Based on the truck’s detected location and speed, the stored trolley-line location, and the raising time, a controller issues a signal indicating when the current-collecting units may be raised.
outputs.L3:
An electric-drive dump truck receives electrical power from overhead trolley lines through movable power collection units. These power collection units are raised and lowered by dedicated lifting devices, allowing them to contact the trolley lines when external power is available and to retract when contact is unnecessary or unsafe.

Detection devices continuously monitor the dump truck’s current position and traveling speed. A storage section retains information indicating the location of the trolley lines, as well as the amount of time required for the lifting devices to raise the power collection units into contact with those lines.

Using the truck’s detected position and speed, the stored trolley-line location, and the required raising time, a control device determines the appropriate timing for initiating the lifting operation. The control device then outputs a signal indicating when the power collection units may be safely raised, enabling them to reach the trolley lines at the proper point along the truck’s travel path.
outputs.L4:
An electric-drive dump truck is equipped with power collection units that can be raised to contact overhead trolley lines while the truck is traveling. A position detector determines the truck’s current location, and a speed detector measures its traveling speed. A controller also stores information identifying the locations at which trolley lines begin along the truck’s route, together with the time required for the power collection units to move from their lowered positions to positions where they can contact the lines.

Using the detected position and speed, the controller calculates the distance the truck will travel during the lifting operation. It then determines a lifting-start point located sufficiently before the beginning of the trolley line so that the power collection units reach the required contact height at an appropriate location beneath the line. When the truck reaches this safe lifting point, the controller outputs a signal instructing the power collection units to rise.

By accounting for both vehicle motion and the collectors’ lifting time, the system prevents the collectors from being raised too early or too late. The collectors can therefore engage the trolley lines reliably while the dump truck remains in motion, reducing missed contact, mechanical impact, and operational interruptions while enabling a smooth transition to power supplied from the overhead lines.
outputs.L5:
## An Electric Drive

An electric drive is a system that converts electrical energy into mechanical motion. It usually consists of an electric motor, a power converter, a controller, and a power source such as a battery or the electrical grid. These components work together to regulate speed, torque, and direction.

Electric drives are widely used in industrial machines, household appliances, elevators, trains, and electric vehicles. Compared with combustion engines, they are highly efficient, quiet, and easy to control. They also require less maintenance because electric motors contain fewer moving parts.

In electric vehicles, the battery supplies energy to the motor through a power electronic converter. The controller adjusts the flow of electricity according to the driver’s commands. During braking, many electric drives can recover energy and return it to the battery through regenerative braking.

Electric drives are an important part of modern technology. They help reduce energy consumption and local emissions, especially when powered by renewable electricity. As batteries, motors, and control systems continue to improve, electric drives will play an increasingly significant role in sustainable transportation and industrial automation.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a patent-style abstract describing an electric drive dump truck that automatically determines when its power collection units can be raised to contact trolley lines.
counterfactuals.output: An electric drive dump truck includes an electric propulsion system, an onboard electrical power source, and one or more selectively raisable power collection units configured to contact overhead trolley lines. A control system automatically determines whether conditions permit raising the power collection units. The control system receives signals indicative of vehicle position, heading, speed, steering angle, lateral alignment with the trolley lines, trolley-line presence, and/or an operating state of the truck. Based on the signals and stored information defining a trolley-enabled travel region, the control system determines whether each power collection unit is positioned within an allowable contact envelope and whether applicable raising criteria are satisfied. When the criteria are satisfied, the control system commands an actuator to raise the corresponding power collection unit into electrical contact with a trolley line, thereby supplying electrical power to the propulsion system. The control system may inhibit or discontinue raising, or lower a power collection unit, when the truck is outside the trolley-enabled region, is improperly aligned, exceeds a threshold speed or steering condition, detects an obstruction or fault, or otherwise fails to satisfy the raising criteria. The disclosed arrangement facilitates automatic, safe engagement with trolley lines during haulage operations.

counterfactuals.output: The invention is a control system for a trolley-powered dump truck that automatically raises its pantograph at the correct point beneath an overhead trolley line. The system detects the truck’s current position and speed, references stored data identifying the trolley-line location, and accounts for the time required to lift the pantograph. It calculates when lifting should begin so the pantograph reaches operating height as the truck enters the trolley-line section, enabling reliable electrical connection without requiring precise manual operation.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a technical description of a control system that signals when a moving electric dump truck’s power collectors should be raised so they contact overhead trolley lines at the correct time.
counterfactuals.output:
### Control System for Timing Engagement of Power Collectors with Overhead Trolley Lines

The control system determines when a moving electric dump truck has entered a suitable trolley-line engagement zone and generates a command or operator indication to raise the truck’s power collectors. The timing accounts for vehicle motion and collector deployment time so that the collector heads reach operating height after passing the leading end of the trolley lines and while positioned beneath a valid contact region.

The system includes:

- a vehicle-position sensor, such as GNSS, RFID, magnetic markers, optical markers, or roadside transponders;
- a vehicle-speed and direction input obtained from wheel-speed sensors, the traction controller, or an inertial measurement unit;
- one or more overhead-line detectors, such as cameras, lidar, radar, inductive sensors, or electric-field sensors;
- a stored map defining trolley-line entry points, engagement zones, and exclusion zones;
- a collector-position sensor indicating lowered, deploying, raised, or faulted status; and
- a controller connected to the sensors, the vehicle control network, and an operator display or automatic collector actuator.

As the truck approaches a trolley section, the controller estimates the truck’s distance to the start of the usable contact zone and calculates a predicted arrival time:

\[
t_{\text{arrival}}=\frac{d_{\text{entry}}}{v}
\]

where \(d_{\text{entry}}\) is the distance to the selected engagement point and \(v\) is the truck’s current or predicted speed. The controller compares this value with the collector deployment time, including compensation for actuator delay, vehicle acceleration, road grade, suspension movement, position uncertainty, and a configurable safety margin.

A raise signal is generated when:

\[
t_{\text{arrival}} \leq t_{\text{deploy}}+t_{\text{delay}}+t_{\text{margin}}
\]

provided that all enabling conditions are satisfied. These conditions may include confirmation that the truck is traveling in the permitted direction, its lateral position is within the trolley corridor, its speed is within an allowable range, the overhead conductors have been detected, sufficient usable line length remains, and no bridge, crossover, switch, broken-wire area, maintenance zone, or other exclusion region is present.

The commanded engagement point is selected so that the collector heads do not rise into the leading ends, support hardware, or non-contact portions of the trolley installation. If vehicle speed changes during deployment, the controller updates the predicted contact location and may advance, delay, or cancel the raise request. A confidence value can be calculated from map position, line detection, lateral alignment, and sensor integrity. Automatic raising is permitted only above a specified confidence threshold; otherwise, the system provides an advisory indication to the operator or inhibits engagement.

The output may be:

1. a visual, audible, or haptic “raise collectors” indication to the operator;
2. an enable signal requiring operator confirmation; or
3. an automatic raise command to the collector actuator.

Following issuance of the signal, the controller monitors collector motion and verifies successful line contact using collector-height feedback, contact-force sensing, line-voltage detection, arc detection, or current-flow confirmation. If contact is not established within a specified interval, or if alignment is lost, the controller commands the collectors to lower and records a diagnostic fault.

The system is fail-safe. Loss of position data, implausible speed information, conflicting line-detection inputs, actuator faults, excessive vehicle roll or lateral offset, or communication failure suppresses the automatic raise command. The controller also maintains event logs containing vehicle position, speed, calculated deployment point, sensor confidence, collector status, and contact results for maintenance and system optimization.
